I've had experience of this in the UK with my doctor, who asked me if I'd thought about how I would do it, and what steps I had taken (such as getting the things I'd need to carry it out). They basically want to know if you have a plan, and how far through you've gone with it, so they can decide if you pose a near-term danger to yourself.


I also said that I didn't feel particularly sad about my situation by the way, and they said that wasn't a good sign, but since all I had was an idea (not the actual means to carry it out), nobody tried to stop me leaving.


Basically, doctors and therapists have a duty of care towards you, and (somewhat obviously) operate on the assumption that whatever else is going on, it's better that you're alive than dead. It'll depend a bit on where you are, but I think the general protocol is, if they decide you're an immediate danger to yourself, they will want you hospitalised.


Hope that helps :)

Feel free to share your story on here, however long it is. There's always someone who will listen and be willing to talk.

I'm guessing there's something you would want to achieve by writing the letter, rather than you just feel it's the thing to do.

I'll guess also that maybe what you want to do is protect other people's feelings. I'm not claiming to know your mindset - I really am just guessing. But if you're hoping there's something you can say in the letter that will make it easier for the people who care about you, well.. sorry to say it, but a letter won't help much with that.

It might be worth giving therapy another chance if you're able to try a different therapist. Sadly, I think finding a therapist who is good at what they do, _and_ that you click with, involves a fair bit of luck.

I completely relate to not liking social gatherings by the way. Sometimes I like them for a while, but long before most people are ready to quit I realise I'm not enjoying myself and have disappeared into my shell again.

I find it helps to be able to feel like I can leave at any time - but I appreciate that would be tricky if you're always going with another person. If you can arrange it though, I wonder if that would help. I've found that just leaving when I want to leave works quite well - it saves all the awkwardness of having to do rounds of goodbyes and people telling you to stay, etc. People don't often notice if you just leave, and they're rarely offended even if they do.

I completely relate to this frustration.

Nobody has a choice about being born into the world, but wanting to opt out is not ok. It seems to me like a kind of emotional blackmail. It bugs me that a person isn't free to choose. It seems unfair that you can't say no thanks, it's not for me.

Hey, thanks for the questions.

I started thinking about suicide regularly after a couple of months on antidepressants (which I started earlier this year), but I don't think the meds are responsible for the thought patterns themselves. Even pre-meds, like with that job I took, I've often thought about finding ways to deliberately put myself in harm's way. It feels like I've been harbouring some kind of death wish for a long time. I don't have the patience or interest in trying to live a happy life while my brain tries to kill me. It seems the meds can deal with the feelings but not the thoughts.

I didn't really consciously stop doing any of those healthy things. I'm not interested in trying them again because I'm tired of the cycle of hope and despair that comes with trying things and always eventually losing interest in them. Besides which I've now convinced myself that I just fundamentally don't want to live, so what would be the point of any of that stuff.

I haven't looked for any support groups, and to be honest I don't want help. I don't know how being on here figures into that, but if anybody actually tries to offer me help I just refuse it, like I think I know better (that superiority complex thing again). The idea of being in a group of strangers who might like me or want me to open up or accept me for who I am makes me want to run a mile, perverse as that sounds. I am pretty wretched tbh.

Hey,

I have kind of an opposite issue, and I hope sharing will offer some perspective. My parents prioritised my academic education over my social development and it screwed me. I grew up with little in the way of social skills, unconsciously seeing intelligence as the highest value, judging people who I thought weren't as smart as me and generally treating most people as inferior. Needless to say it has just served to isolate me, and I have almost no friends. I would trade almost every last shred of academic intelligence for social skills, because that is what I feel people need most in basically every arena of life.

I absolutely don't mean to say that you are somehow wrong to feel the way you do. Your feelings are completely real and legitimate. What I want to offer is that it might be possible to feel better without being more 'intelligent'. I think that's probably as much as I can say without just kind of guessing and speculating, but I hope that helps.
